annotations.text: Settings lives in the match and nowhere else; the landing keeps saying only who, where and what. So the whole question is the in-game menu: leave, change sides, settings, one system for mouse, keyboard, controller and touch. One honest constraint under every board: nothing pauses in a shared arena, so a menu is something you open while the fight goes on.

The landing column's grammar carried into the match: stops for LEAVE, SETTINGS and SIDE, RESUME breathing where PLAY NOW breathes at home. Same muscle memory everywhere, targets big enough for a thumb. The dim is deliberately thin so the fight stays half-visible behind it.
The settings stop opens the way the ship stop opens at home: the panel climbs from its row. Since this is the only home settings has, the panel is the drawer's whole settings page, bands and all.

The direction that most respects the no-pause truth: the corner key docks a panel and the fight stays live and undimmed beside it. Nothing is hidden while you fiddle. On a phone, though, the live fight is exactly what a stray thumb hits.
The shape every console game has taught: four rows in the middle of a dimmed screen. Compact, but settings becomes a second page in place, one level deeper than the column version needs.

Hold the key and four choices ring your own ship; flick toward one and let go. Fastest on a stick or a thumb and invisible until held, but it is the one direction that costs a new grammar to learn, and settings still needs a panel after the flick. Drawn to bound the space.
